So, what are you learning? Any simple secrets you could share with an amateur?

Here's one that I was totally missing: More EQ. Then add more. Start with small broad tweaks on the mix bus to get closer to your reference. Then solo each track and do a sweep with a narrow Q to find room resonance, then drop those frequencies a couple of DB in a surgical fashion. Then, add your compression, then another EQ for broader tweaks. You may even have a few tracks together on a bus with even more EQ. Only use solo when identifying room resonances in your track, as your ultimate goal is to make all of the tracks work together, not get the best sound out of an individual track. I was trying to approach each track with a single EQ. I was trying to do too much with one EQ.

Are you saying that you EQ the whole mix when it's combined? That's something I never even thought of, though I should have. I been just EQing the individual tracks to try to get them to sound nice. I can't believe I never thought of doing it to the whole thing

Yes, that's the mix bus. Start there. Load in a reference track (something you'd like it to sound similar to) and compare your mix to it. Start with broad, small adjustments to the mix bus, then use a fully parametric EQ on the individual tracks with the sweep/cut technique to remove room resonances, then add another EQ to tweak it to your liking. Also understand that you don't want too much energy in the same spot. If the guitars are strong at 200hz, and so is the bass guitar, cut one of them a tad to allow room for the other. Rock music is super heavy in the 200-500hz range, so you have to allocate space for each instrument to sit.
That's kind of what I do with the EQ, I try to get each track it's own band accentuated, to help each instrument be able to be heard. I love the advice thanks!

Ive read about a plugin that allows you to see the EQ curve of a reference track. That’s a tool I need to look into. I agree that an overall EQ applied to the Master is the best place to start. You might otherwise be notching a room frequency at say 4K on every damn track otherwise. I’ve been happy on my last 2 tracks applying a master EQ with a high pass at 20hz to kill all the sub frequencies and unnecessary low end, and a high shelf boosting a few dB around 7k-20k. It’s past the guitar speaker range but helps the vocals pop a little and adds some sparkle to the symbols and high hat

That's basically just a spectrum analyzer. It's really useful for seeing where the energy is in your mixes. There should be one in your DAW. Some EQ's have them built in. I am researching Up On Cripple Creek, 'cause we're going to try to add it to the set list for next weekend. I have the tab and sheet music for all the instruments - except one. I can find no official source for it.

Through some research, I have deduced that the "Jaw" (sometimes "Jew/Jew's") Harp is actually a clavinet with a wah wah pedal. I have faked it with a guitar before but I now have a band with 5 other talented musicians and want to make the reproduction even more faithful. So, I started digging into it. I'm about 80% positive that the keyboards the two keys players (there's overlap and some songs have multiple keys in them) have have a 'clavinet' setting.

I've further deduced that it is a Honer Clavinet D6 but I am not sure what specific wah pedal was used. Our main keyboard player should be able to pull off both that and the organ, 'cause that is how Garth Hudson did it. A careful ear will note that the clavinet ends just as the organ begins.

I figure you'll like that trivia. So, it's a mid-morning treasure!
